strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and addresses a real bottleneck: applying RL to dense 3D registration by defining the policy over the encoder latent space rather than the million-dimensional deformation field, which sidesteps the memory/sampling problems that have confined prior RL registration methods to low-dimensional actions.

The paper provides an unusually thorough empirical validation: three 3D benchmarks (OASIS, LiTS, Abdomen MR-CT), three refactorable backbones (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans), comparison against multiple recent strong baselines (CorrMLP, RIIR, WarpDDF+RegCut, SPAC), Wilcoxon significance testing, trajectory/step ablations (Table 2), component-wise ablations (Table 3), label-efficiency curves (Fig. 4), warm-up analysis (Fig. 5), and parameter/latency overhead analysis (Table 4).

The component ablation (Table 3) is informative: multi-step refinement without GRPO actually degrades NJD (e.g., VoxelMorph-L 0.32 to 0.37), while the full GRPO configuration improves both Dice (~+1.7 to ~+2.5) and NJD substantially (0.32 to 0.10), supporting the claim that stochastic policy optimization adds value beyond simply cascading a weakly supervised model.

LDVN is cleanly justified: the derivation that scaling log-likelihoods by 1/s preserves advantage ordering and gradient direction (Eq. 13), plus the O(N) variance argument for choosing s ∝ √N, is simple but correct, and the clarification that LDVN does not alter the sampling distribution or temperature is a nice touch.
The overhead analysis (Table 4) demonstrates the practicality claims: <3% extra parameters, minimal single-step latency cost, and an explicit accuracy-latency trade-off for multi-step inference.
weaknesses: A critical ambiguity surrounds inference-time trajectory selection. Eq. 9 defines the reward using Dice(Sf, Sm∘Φ) with ground-truth segmentation labels, and the paper states trajectories are greedily selected by highest reward at the end of each step (Eq. 17-18). If this selection also occurs at test time, the method uses ground-truth labels at inference, which would materially undermine the fairness of the reported comparisons; if selection instead uses a label-free surrogate at test time, this is never stated and should be explicit. This needs clarification before the results can be fully trusted.

The contribution of GRPO itself over simply training the baseline with a weakly supervised Dice loss is modest: Table 3 shows the jump from unsupervised to Dice-loss training accounts for roughly 9-10 Dice points, while adding the full GRPO machinery contributes ~1.7-2.5 points on top. The headline framing emphasizes the RL paradigm, but most of the gain comes from the weak supervision that baselines also receive.

Novelty is incremental at the component level: GRPO is adopted from DeepSeek-Math/R1, the Gaussian head with reparameterization is a standard VAE-style construction, and coarse-to-fine step-wise registration is well established (LapIRN, ULAE-Net, cascades). The genuinely new element, LDVN, amounts to dividing log-likelihood sums by √N — a textbook variance normalization — yet it is billed as 'the first general statistical normalization scheme that stabilizes GRPO,' which overstates a fairly routine trick.

There are internal inconsistencies in reported numbers that suggest hasty writing: Section 5.1 claims 'Dice increases by 23%' on OASIS, but Table 1 shows ~2.4 absolute points (84.77 to 87.16, ~2.8% relative); the conclusion repeats 'Dice improvements on the order of 24%.' These should read 2-4%, and such errors erode confidence in the quantitative reporting.

The unbiasedness and stability claims for LDVN are supported only by an informal asymptotic argument ('bounded second moments and weak dependence') with details deferred to an appendix that is not present in the main text; key experimental details (loss formulations, hyperparameters, hardware) are likewise relegated to a supplement not included, limiting the self-containedness and verifiability of the work.

The claim of 'optimizer-agnostic' and 'backbone-agnostic' generality is supported only for GRPO on three U-Net/transformer variants within the same encoder-decoder family; no evidence is given for other optimizers or genuinely different architectures, and the method requires a widened VoxelMorph-L (27M parameters) specifically to make the latent space expressive enough, which somewhat contradicts the minimal-cost framing.

Baseline fairness is mostly handled well, but MorphSeek uses multi-step (3-step) inference while most baselines are single-pass; RIIR (Steps=12) and SPAC (Steps=20) are the only multi-step comparisons, and the interaction between trajectory sampling (J=6 per step) and the reported inference latency is not clearly separated from the stepwise composition cost.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and well-motivated gap: applying RL-based step-wise optimization to 3D deformable registration while avoiding the intractable million-dimensional action space, by defining the policy over encoder latent features instead of the dense deformation field.

Evaluation breadth is reasonably good: three 3D benchmarks (OASIS, LiTS, Abdomen MR-CT, including a cross-modality task) and three backbones (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans), with Wilcoxon significance testing, support the claim that the paradigm is backbone-agnostic.

Component-wise ablation (Table 3) and trajectory/step ablation (Table 2) are informative, and the warm-up analysis (Fig. 5) with an honest statement that warm-up reduces cost/instability rather than raising the performance ceiling is commendably candid.
Overhead analysis (Table 4) shows the refactor is lightweight (<3% parameters), and the label-efficiency analysis (Fig. 4) addresses the practical weakly-supervised scenario directly.
The LDVN variance analysis (s ∝ √N keeping std of relative log-likelihoods O(1)) is a simple but sensible statistical treatment of the high-dimensional log-likelihood problem.
weaknesses: The necessity of the RL machinery is not convincingly established by the authors' own ablation. In Table 3, moving from '+Dice loss' (84.87) to '+Multi-step' (85.50) to '+GRPO' (87.16) on VoxelMorph-L shows the GRPO component adds roughly 1.5 Dice points over a multi-step weakly-supervised baseline that already uses the same labels. The paper does not compare against the obvious simpler alternative: multi-step inference with the same weakly-supervised network re-optimized per step, or simply ensembling/test-time stochastic sampling. This weakens the central claim that group-relative policy optimization is the key mechanism.

The novelty claim that LDVN is 'the first general statistical normalization scheme' for GRPO is overstated. Dividing the summed log-likelihood by √N is a straightforward variance-stabilization trick, and the 'unbiasedness' argument (Eq. 13) actually shows only that LDVN is equivalent to a step-size rescaling — it changes the effective learning rate, which is an optimization property, not evidence of estimator unbiasedness in a meaningful sense.

There are serious numerical inconsistencies and apparent errors in the results narrative. Section 5.1 claims 'Dice increases by 23%' on OASIS, but Table 1 shows 84.77→87.16 (about 2.4 points, ~2.8% relative); the conclusion similarly states 'Dice improvements on the order of 24%' and 'NJD reductions of roughly 3060%', which appear to be garbled versions of 2–4% and 30–60%. Such errors in the headline claims undermine confidence in the reported results. Additionally, the baseline Dice in Table 3 (e.g., TransMorph 76.84) differs substantially from Table 1 (85.89) without a clear explanation of the configuration difference.

Comparison fairness is only partially assured. MorphSeek uses multi-step (3-step) inference with ~3x latency while several baselines are single-shot, and the reward uses the test-time Dice metric with hard labels; although baselines use the same weak supervision, the asymmetric step budgets and the best-of-J trajectory selection at each step (Eqs. 17–18) are not ablated against a non-RL greedy multi-step search.

Test sets are very small (19 pairs for OASIS, 8 paired scans for Abdomen MR-CT), and only Dice/NJD are reported — no landmark-based TRE or boundary metrics, which limits the evidence for the claimed improvement in 'local geometric consistency'.

Key details are deferred to a supplement that is not included (hyperparameters, loss instantiations, LDVN derivation, SPAC NJD explanation), and no code release is mentioned, hurting reproducibility for a method with many interacting components (τ, s, J, T, KL trust-region schedule, λ warm/λ Dice).

Writing quality is below venue standard: several equations have malformed notation (Eq. 12 denominator, clipped log σ ranges without units/values), typos ('3060%', '23%'), and inconsistent claims between abstract, results, and conclusion.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel for the registration literature: instead of forcing RL to operate in the million-dimensional dense DVF space (which prior work like Krebs et al. and SPAC had to aggressively compress, losing spatial detail), MorphSeek defines the stochastic policy over the encoder's top-level latent features, sidestepping the dimensionality bottleneck while retaining fine granularity. This is a well-motivated and clean reframing.

The LDVN analysis, while simple, is a useful practical contribution: the observation that summing log-likelihoods over tens of thousands of latent dimensions inflates within-group variance and destabilizes GRPO is insightful, the s∝√N scaling is statistically justified (Var of the sum is O(N) under weak dependence), and the unbiasedness argument (Eq. 13) is correct — the rescaling preserves ordering and acts as a step-size change on the policy gradient.

Empirical support is broad: three 3D benchmarks (OASIS, LiTS, Abdomen MR←CT, including a challenging cross-modality task) and three backbones (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans), with statistically significant improvements over each backbone (Wilcoxon p<0.05) in most cases. MorphSeek also surpasses strong recent methods (CorrMLP on OASIS/LiTS, RIIR on most tasks), which strengthens the case beyond mere incremental improvement over its own backbones.

The ablations are thorough and informative: the trajectory/step grid (Table 2) supports the coarse-to-fine interpretation with a clear saturation/artifact pattern; the component ablation (Table 3) isolates the Gaussian head (negligible alone), Dice supervision, multi-step, and GRPO contributions; Table 4 quantifies the modest overhead (<3% parameters, ~2.5x latency for 3 steps); Figure 4 demonstrates genuine label efficiency (98.5% of full-label performance with 60% of labels).

The multi-trajectory sampling + greedy best-trajectory state update is a sensible way to reuse scarce labels across refinement steps, and the fixed-prior KL trust region against N(0,I) is a reasonable critic-free alternative to PPO ratios in this high-dimensional setting.
weaknesses: There is a misleading quantitative claim: Section 5.1 and Section 5.4 state 'Dice increases by 23%' (presumably meaning 2–3 percentage points), and 'Dice improvements on the order of 2–4%' elsewhere; the abstract and text should be internally consistent, and percentage-point framing should be used explicitly. Similar sloppiness appears in '3060%' (30–60%) and 'NICE-Trans page 750760'. These typos undermine confidence in careful reporting.

Fairness of the head-to-head comparison deserves more discussion: MorphSeek performs multi-step, multi-trajectory inference while most baselines are single-shot. The authors do include multi-step baselines (RIIR Steps=12, SPAC Steps=20), which mitigates this, but a single-step MorphSeek ablation or a matched-step comparison against cascade baselines (e.g., ULAE-Net, LapIRN) under the same weak supervision would make the attribution to the policy mechanism crisper.

Inconsistency between Table 3 and Table 1 baselines is confusing: Table 3 row 1 (VoxelMorph-L baseline, no weak supervision) reports 75.31 Dice, while Table 1's weakly-supervised VoxelMorph-L is 84.77. The table is internally consistent (row 3 with Dice loss gives 84.87), but the baseline definition differences should be stated explicitly, and it raises the question of whether the appropriate reference for the GRPO gain is 84.77 rather than 75.31.

The claimed label-efficiency gains partly conflate two effects: the soft-Dice loss (Eq. 15) is a direct supervised objective that any baseline could also use, and Figure 4 compares 'TransMorph (supervised)' against 'TransMorph w. MorphSeek' without clarifying whether the baseline receives the same number of gradient updates per labeled pair. The efficiency claim would be stronger with a baseline trained with matched multi-step Dice losses.

Some overclaiming: 'the first general statistical normalization scheme that stabilizes GRPO in high-dimensional dense prediction settings' is too strong given that variance-controlled likelihood normalization is closely related to existing practice; LDVN's unbiasedness proof is essentially the observation that a positive rescaling of log-likelihood ratios does not change the gradient direction, which is straightforward.

The Abdomen MR←CT test set contains only 8 paired scans, so the reported gains (e.g., +4.1 Dice for TransMorph) rest on a very small sample; the Wilcoxon test on 8 pairs is fragile. Additionally, NICE-Trans NJD on OASIS is unchanged (0.02→0.02), so the blanket claim of 'NJD reductions of roughly 30–60%' does not hold universally.

Reproducibility is limited in the main text: key hyperparameters (T, τ, λscale, λreg, βKL, λwarm, λDice, target-KL schedule) are deferred to a supplement, and no code release is mentioned. Given the training complexity (three stages, group sampling), a code release would substantially strengthen the contribution.

The theoretical analysis of s∝√N assumes 'bounded second moments and weak dependence' among the summation terms, which is plausible for Gaussian i.i.d. components but stated without proof in the main text; the appendix derivation is not shown to hold under the actual correlated spatial structure of the latent field.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: RL-based registration has been limited to low-dimensional action spaces, and the idea of placing a stochastic Gaussian policy head in the encoder latent space (rather than the million-dimensional deformation field) is a sensible and non-trivial reformulation that retains fine spatial granularity while keeping sampling tractable.

Experimental coverage is unusually thorough: three 3D benchmarks (OASIS, LiTS, cross-modality Abdomen MR–CT), three backbones (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans), statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<0.05), classical optimization baselines (SyN, deedsBCV), multi-stage baselines (RIIR, LapIRN), and label-efficiency curves.

The component ablation (Table 3) and trajectory/step ablation (Table 2) cleanly isolate the contribution of each part (Gaussian head, Dice loss, multi-step, GRPO), supporting the claim that GRPO is the key mechanism coupling weak supervision with step-wise refinement.

The LDVN analysis is supported by both theory (Proposition 1 on affine invariance of the policy gradient under zero-mean advantages) and empirical verification (Monte Carlo check of the weak-dependence assumption, ratio 1.01±0.04; scaling-factor ablation s∈{1,√N,N}).

The supplementary analysis of why NJD cannot be reliably reported for SPAC (post-hoc composition causing >10% Dice drop, Table 9) demonstrates scientific care rather than silently omitting an unfavorable comparison.

Warm-up analysis is convincing: 20-run stability statistics (success rate 33%→79%, convergence 120→75 epochs) plus a posterior-collapse probe (Table 6) substantiate the role of deterministic warm-up, and hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 5) is honestly reported, including failure modes.
The paper is well-written and the supplement contains sufficient detail (losses, reward shaping, splits, hyperparameters, hardware) for reproduction.
weaknesses: Test sets are small: 19 pairs on OASIS, 40 on LiTS, and only 8 paired scans on the Abdomen MR–CT task. For the 8-pair test set, reported gains (e.g., 86.49 vs 82.37 Dice) rest on very few cases and per-case variance is large (±3.35 on 8 samples), which limits the strength of cross-modality conclusions.

LDVN's practical novelty is modest. The paper itself proves (Proposition 1) that the transform only rescales gradient magnitude by a positive constant, so much of its effect is equivalent to learning-rate adjustment; the residual benefit (gradient variance stabilization) is real but thin, and the paper would benefit from a direct comparison against simply rescaling the policy learning rate.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is high: the exploration temperature τ must be annealed from 10 to 2, and τ=15 collapses performance to 55.67 Dice; σ clipping is essential (no clip → 33.05 Dice). This fragility somewhat undercuts the claim of a 'principled, backbone-agnostic' solution, and the paper provides limited principled guidance for choosing these values on new tasks/domains.

The label-efficiency claim is evaluated only on OASIS with one backbone (TransMorph); it is unclear whether the strong low-label behavior (near-full performance at 60% of labels) transfers to the larger-deformation abdominal tasks.

Multi-step inference requires T forward passes (roughly 3× latency at the default configuration), and training requires J=6 samples per state; while efficiency is reported, the practical cost of the approach relative to single-shot baselines is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed against accuracy-per-FLOP trade-offs with competing multi-stage methods.

Some comparisons are not fully unified: CorrMLP, RIIR, SPAC, and WarpDDF+RegCut are evaluated under their published protocols rather than the unified weakly supervised setting, so the fairness of those rows in Table 1 is imperfect, though the strongest comparisons (refactored backbones with identical labels) are fair.
No explicit statement of code release, which, given the numerous dataset-specific preprocessing and pair-construction choices, slightly hinders reproducibility.
The claimed generality to 'other dense correspondence problems' is asserted only in the conclusion and not demonstrated.

strengths: The core idea is reasonably novel for the registration literature: reformulating RL-based DIR so that the policy acts on a sampleable high-resolution encoder latent rather than on a low-dimensional parametrization (Krebs et al., SPAC) or on the dense deformation field, retaining spatial granularity while avoiding a million-dimensional action space.

The empirical evaluation is broad and fairly well controlled: three 3D benchmarks (OASIS, LiTS, cross-modality Abdomen MR-CT), three refactored backbones (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans), comparison against multi-step methods (RIIR, LapIRN-stage3, SPAC, CorrMLP), Wilcoxon significance testing, and an explicit weakly-supervised protocol applied identically to refactored baselines (Table 1).

The ablation package is unusually thorough: trajectory/step ablation (Table 2), component ablation (Table 3), LDVN scaling ablation (Fig. 5), hyperparameter sensitivity including posterior-collapse probes (Tables 5-6), and a warm-up stability analysis over 20 independent runs (33% -> 79% stable-training rate).

The supplementary discussion of why NJD cannot be reliably computed for SPAC (Sec. 9, Table 9) is honest and careful: rather than reporting a misleading metric, the authors explain the interpolation/discretization/non-associativity issues and quantify the >10% Dice degradation of post-hoc field reconstruction.

Label-efficiency claims are supported by a dedicated experiment (Fig. 3: near full performance with ~60 labeled pairs; 98.5% of full-label performance with 60% of the data), and the computational analysis (Table 11) shows <3% parameter overhead and near-linear multi-step latency scaling.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: the framework is essentially a VAE-style Gaussian head (reparameterized sampling, KL to N(0,I)) combined with GRPO, and LDVN reduces to dividing the group-relative log-likelihood by sqrt(N). The theoretical analysis (Prop. 1, variance argument in Sec. 7.1) is mathematically straightforward - affine invariance under zero-mean advantages is a near-trivial consequence of sum(A)=0 - so the 'theoretical contribution' framing feels overstated.

The inference procedure is under-specified. During fine-tuning, state updates use a greedy best-of-J selection based on a reward that requires ground-truth segmentations (Eqs. 9, 16-17, Algorithm 1). The paper does not clearly state how trajectory selection is done at test time (deterministic z=mu? single trajectory? label-free?). Since test-time latency is claimed to be close to the original model, some selection mechanism must be assumed, but this materially affects both the method's applicability (label-free inference?) and the reported numbers.

Training cost is not adequately reported. Multi-trajectory GRPO with J=6, T=3 steps means ~18 decoder passes plus J forward passes per labeled pair per step; only inference latency (Table 11) is given. Given that the method's selling point is efficiency under memory/label budgets, total GRPO training time and memory versus the supervised baselines should be quantified; the OOM at 8 trajectories (Table 2) suggests the cost is non-trivial.

Evaluation relies almost exclusively on Dice and NJD. No TRE, HD95, or landmark-based metrics are reported, which are standard in registration evaluation; with only 19/40/8 test pairs (the Abdomen MR-CT test set has just 8 scans), the statistical strength of the cross-modality claims is limited.

Minor inconsistencies and deferred content reduce clarity: Table 3's 'Baseline' Dice (e.g., 75.31 for VoxelMorph-L) differs substantially from Table 1's VoxelMorph-L (84.77) without immediate explanation (presumably unsupervised vs. weakly supervised), which could confuse readers; key analyses (LDVN derivation, ablations, architecture details) are relegated to the supplement, leaving the main paper's central claims incompletely supported in isolation.

No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a multi-stage training pipeline (warm-up, GRPO, temperature annealing, many interacting hyperparameters) whose stability the authors themselves show is sensitive (Table 5: Dice ranges from 33.05 to 89.52 under hyperparameter deviations).

Overclaiming in language: phrases like 'optimizer-agnostic' and 'backbone-agnostic paradigm for scalable visual alignment' generalize beyond what is demonstrated (one RL optimizer, three registration backbones, three datasets).

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly positioned: existing RL-based registration either restricts action spaces to low-dimensional rigid/PCA-parameterized transforms (Krebs et al.) or compresses to very low-dimensional plans (SPAC), while treating the full 3D dense field as the action is computationally prohibitive. Placing the stochastic policy in the top-level encoder latent space is a sensible and seemingly novel resolution of this bottleneck, and it is demonstrated to be backbone-agnostic (VoxelMorph-L, TransMorph, NICE-Trans).

Consistent, statistically supported empirical gains: Dice improvements of ~2-4% and NJD reductions of ~30-60% across three 3D benchmarks (OASIS, LiTS, cross-modality Abdomen MR-CT) and three backbones, with Wilcoxon signed-rank significance tests reported against each refactored baseline (Table 1). The method also outperforms multi-stage alternatives (RIIR, LapIRN-stage3 under the same 100-pair label setting, Table 7).

The evaluation includes the critical ablation that isolates the RL contribution (Table 3): adding a weakly supervised Dice loss alone (row 3) and multi-step alone (row 4) are compared against the full GRPO configuration (row 5), which shows GRPO adds meaningful Dice gains and a large NJD reduction. This directly addresses the most obvious confound, i.e., that gains might come from multi-step fine-tuning plus Dice loss rather than policy optimization.

The LDVN analysis is a nice touch: the supplement proves that the affine rescaling preserves the policy-gradient direction under zero-mean advantages (Proposition 1), derives the O(sqrt(N)) growth of log-likelihood std under weak dependence, verifies the weak-dependence assumption empirically (variance ratio 1.01±0.04), and ablates s ∈ {1, sqrt(N), N} (Figure 5).

Strong label-efficiency analysis: Figure 3 shows strong gains from ~16 labeled pairs and near-full performance at ~60% of labels, and the T×J relative supervision events per labeled pair provide a plausible mechanism for why label efficiency improves.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough and honest: posterior-collapse analysis, warm-up stability statistics (33%→79% stable-training rate over 20 runs), hyperparameter sensitivity including failure modes, the reward-hacking failure case when removing L_warm, and a careful, well-argued explanation of why NJD cannot be reliably reported for SPAC (Table 9) rather than silently omitting it.
Efficiency is credibly reported: <3% parameter overhead and quantified per-step inference latency (Table 11), with the accuracy/runtime trade-off of multi-step inference made explicit.

The paper is well written overall; the method section is precise, and the supplement contains sufficient implementation detail (losses, splits, pair construction, hyperparameters, hardware) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The conceptual depth of the RL contribution is debatable. Since L_Dice (Eq. 14) provides direct, differentiable weak supervision on the same quantities the reward measures, the GRPO component functions largely as a stochastic multi-hypothesis ranking scheme layered on top of standard weakly supervised fine-tuning. The paper argues this smooths the non-convex landscape (Sec. 10.2), but no comparison is made against simpler alternatives that might capture similar benefits, e.g., test-time sampling/ensembling of the deterministic model, stochastic weight averaging, or plain multi-step self-training. Without such baselines, the necessity of the full GRPO machinery remains partially open.

The greedy trajectory selection at inference (Eqs. 16-17) requires computing a reward, i.e., ground-truth segmentations, at test time. It is not fully clear how inference is performed on genuinely unlabeled test data (the reported test metrics are against ground truth, but deployment-time behavior without labels is underspecified), and whether the multi-step inference in Table 11 uses sampling or the deterministic mean.

Test sets are small: 19 pairs for OASIS, 40 for LiTS, and only 8 paired scans for Abdomen MR-CT. The cross-modality result (the headline 4%+ gain) rests on 8 test cases, which limits statistical confidence despite the Wilcoxon tests.

Baseline fairness is mixed: CorrMLP, RIIR, SPAC, and WarpDDF+RegCut are evaluated under 'their published protocols' rather than the unified weakly supervised setting, while the U-Net backbones are refactored. Cross-protocol comparisons in Table 1 should be interpreted with caution, though the within-protocol refactored comparisons are sound.

OOM at 8 trajectories (Table 2) exposes a scalability fragility of the approach that is reported but not analyzed; the exploration cost scales poorly with J in high-dimensional latents, which somewhat undercuts the 'scalable' framing.

LDVN, while correctly analyzed, is a fairly simple scaling heuristic (1/sqrt(N), analogous to scaled dot-product attention); its theoretical contribution is modest and the empirical support is limited to one backbone/dataset.

Some claims are over-broad relative to evidence, e.g., 'backbone-agnostic and optimizer-agnostic solution for scalable visual alignment' rests on three registration backbones and does not extend beyond registration, and the '98.5% of full-label performance with 60% of data' figure is specific to TransMorph on OASIS.
